appraisal_events.evidence: Elle usait... de ces brusques sautes de syntaxe... pour réparer ses imprudences; certaines contradictions, certaines retouches qui me semblaient aussi décisives qu'un flagrant délit; et il fallait à tout prix empêcher qu'Albertine pût retrouver au Trocadéro cette connaissance, si bien que Françoise devait la ramener 'contente ou non'.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator frames Albertine as habitually evasive and untrustworthy about her acquaintances, and treats her as someone to be tracked down and brought back regardless of her own wishes, diminishing both her credibility and her autonomy in this passage.

appraisal_events.evidence: La jalousie... n'est pas seulement impuissante à rien découvrir dans les ténèbres qui l'enveloppent, elle est encore un de ces supplices où la tâche est à recommencer sans cesse, comme celle des Danaïdes, comme celle d'Ixion; j'aurais offert n'importe quelle somme à Léa pour qu'elle n'y allât pas.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's own retrospective self-analysis exposes his jealousy as an endless, self-inflicted torment that reduces him to obsessive surveillance, bribery-minded desperation, and helpless physical agitation rather than any position of strength.

status_effects.explanation: Albertine's credibility and freedom of movement are locally diminished by the narrator's suspicion of her habitual evasiveness and by his insistence that she be brought back whether she likes it or not.
The narrator is locally diminished by his own account of jealousy as a compulsive, unwinnable torment that drives him to frantic, undignified control efforts.

ambiguities: The passage closes with Albertine's relief, gratitude-inducing compliance, and an affectionate letter, but this functions as temporary relief and reassurance rather than realized intimacy or narrator-endorsed renewal, so it does not override the dominant negative movement of suspicion and jealous control that governs most of the passage.

The narrator repeatedly stresses his own uncertainty about whether Albertine actually knows or is lying about Léa ('nous ne le savons pas, nous ne le saurons jamais'), which tempers how firmly the diminishment of Albertine's credibility should be read as an established fact versus the narrator's anxious projection.
